promptText: Even though a Dog IS-A Animal fits inheritance naturally, why does the handbook recommend favoring composition over inheritance in general?
options: Inheritance creates a tightly-coupled hierarchy where a change to the parent can silently break subclasses, while composition lets you swap or mock a collaborator without touching the containing class
Inheritance is not supported for interfaces in modern Java, only composition is
Composition automatically gives a class compile-time polymorphism while inheritance only gives runtime polymorphism
Composition allows a class to directly access the private fields of the object it holds a reference to
explanation: A subclass is locked to its parent's contract and exposes the parent's API, so parent changes ripple into every subclass, whereas an object that merely holds a reference to a collaborator (composition) can have that collaborator swapped or mocked freely; the other options misstate how interfaces, polymorphism, and field access actually work.

promptText: Given `String a = new String("Java"); String b = "Java";`, why does `a == b` evaluate to false even though both contain identical characters?
options: new String(...) always allocates a fresh object on the heap outside the String Pool, so a and b reference different objects despite equal content
String literals are never pooled by the JVM, so a and b were never candidates for sharing a reference
== always returns false when comparing any two String objects, regardless of how they were created
b.equals(a) was implicitly evaluated first and returned false because of a hidden case-sensitivity check
explanation: The pooled literal "Java" and the explicitly-new'd String are two distinct heap objects, so == (identity comparison) is false; calling a.intern() would return the pooled reference and make the comparison true. The other options describe real misconceptions: literals ARE pooled, == does not always return false for Strings, and == never delegates to equals().

promptText: Which of these is a genuine consequence of String being immutable, as opposed to a myth about it?
options: The JVM can cache a String's hashCode once and reuse it, which is a major win since Strings are so often used as HashMap keys
Immutability makes string concatenation with += inside a loop cheaper, not more expensive
Immutability means String cannot be used as a HashMap key at all
Immutability was added only to make StringBuilder unnecessary
explanation: Because a String's value can never change, its hash code is computed once and cached, making repeated hashing (as happens constantly with map keys) essentially free; concatenation in a loop is actually made MORE expensive by immutability (each += builds a new object), and immutability is precisely what makes String a safe, popular map key rather than a disqualifying trait.

promptText: A class can implement Comparable only once. Why would you reach for a separate Comparator instead of adding more logic to compareTo()?
options: When you need multiple, interchangeable sort orders (e.g. by name, salary, or joining date) without modifying the entity class itself
Because Comparable cannot be used with primitive fields like int or long
Because compareTo() cannot be called from within a Collections.sort() call
Because Comparator is required before a class can be stored in any collection at all
explanation: Comparable defines a single natural ordering baked into the class; when the desired order varies by context (name vs salary vs date), external Comparator instances let you define as many orderings as needed without touching the domain class, and they compose cleanly with thenComparing/reversed.

promptText: If a method reassigns an object reference parameter to point at a brand-new object (`param = new User()`), why does the caller's original variable remain unaffected?
options: Java passes a copy of the reference value, so reassigning the local copy inside the method has no effect on the caller's original reference
Java passes the actual object by reference, but reassignment inside a method is blocked by the compiler for safety
Objects are passed by value only when they implement Serializable
The garbage collector prevents reassignment of any parameter that still has an external reference
explanation: Java always copies the variable being passed; for an object reference, the copy is still a pointer to the same heap object, so mutating through it IS visible to the caller, but reassigning the local copy to a different object only changes what that local copy points to, leaving the caller's original reference untouched -- proof that Java is pass-by-value even for objects, not true pass-by-reference.

promptText: What is the compiler-enforced difference between a checked exception like IOException and an unchecked exception like NullPointerException?
options: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws; unchecked exceptions (extending RuntimeException) carry no such compiler enforcement
Checked exceptions can only be thrown from within a static method
Unchecked exceptions can never be caught with a catch block
Checked exceptions always terminate the JVM immediately if uncaught, while unchecked ones do not
explanation: The defining distinction is purely a compile-time one: the compiler forces every checked exception to be caught or declared, because it represents a recoverable condition outside the program's control, while unchecked exceptions usually signal a programming bug and are not compiler-enforced.

promptText: Why do most Spring Boot applications prefer custom unchecked (RuntimeException-based) domain exceptions instead of checked exceptions, and how does Spring itself reflect this philosophy?
options: Checked exceptions force boilerplate throws clauses up every layer of the call stack, so Spring wraps low-level checked exceptions like SQLException into its own unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy for cleaner service interfaces
Checked exceptions are deprecated as of Java 8 and can no longer be declared in method signatures
SQLException cannot be caught directly in a try block, so Spring is forced to wrap it
DataAccessException is itself a checked exception, so nothing really changes for the caller
explanation: Checked exceptions clutter service interfaces with throws clauses that ripple through every caller; Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy is unchecked specifically so vendor-specific, checked persistence exceptions can be translated into a consistent runtime exception handled centrally (e.g. via @RestControllerAdvice) rather than declared everywhere.

promptText: Why does the compiler reject a `catch(Exception e)` block placed before a `catch(IOException e)` block on the same try, and what Java 7+ feature offers a cleaner alternative to writing many separate catch blocks?
options: Exception is a supertype of IOException, making the narrower block unreachable; multi-catch syntax like `catch(IOException | SQLException e)` lets you combine handling for unrelated exception types in one block
The compiler only rejects the ordering because IOException must always be alphabetically first among catch clauses
Multi-catch requires all combined exception types to share a common checked superclass other than Exception
There is no compiler restriction on catch order; it only affects which block's log statement executes first
explanation: Because catch blocks are evaluated top to bottom and the first matching type wins, a broader supertype listed first makes the narrower subtype's block unreachable, which is a compile error, not just a runtime quirk; multi-catch lets genuinely unrelated exception types share one handler without violating this ordering rule.

promptText: Before Generics existed, `List list = new ArrayList(); list.add("Java"); list.add(123);` compiled successfully. Why did this only fail later, at the point where code cast an element back to a specific type?
options: Raw types perform no compile-time type checking on what gets added, so heterogeneous elements are accepted silently; the failure only surfaces as a ClassCastException when incompatible data is later cast to the wrong type
The JVM silently converts the Integer 123 into a String before insertion, so no error ever actually occurs
ArrayList validates every inserted element against the type of the first element added, rejecting mismatches immediately
Raw-typed collections can only ever hold instances of java.lang.Object, so add("Java") itself should have failed to compile
explanation: A raw-typed collection accepts anything because there is no compile-time type parameter to check against; the type mismatch only becomes visible when calling code casts a retrieved element to an incompatible type, producing a runtime ClassCastException -- exactly the class of bug Generics was introduced to catch at compile time instead.

promptText: In a `User -> Address` object graph, why can a shallow copy of a cached User silently corrupt data for every other caller of that cache?
options: A shallow copy duplicates the top-level User but keeps sharing the same nested Address reference, so mutating the Address through one copy changes it for the original and every other holder of that reference
A shallow copy always throws an exception when the object contains any nested reference type
Shallow copies are actually independent of the original in every respect except primitive fields
Deep copies and shallow copies behave identically for objects that override equals()
explanation: Because a shallow copy only duplicates the outer object and copies references (not the referenced objects) for nested fields, both the cached original and the copy point at the same Address; a caller who thinks they have an isolated copy can inadvertently mutate shared state, which is why a genuine deep copy (independent nested objects) is needed when isolation matters.

promptText: What is the distinct role of `transient` versus `serialVersionUID` in Java serialization?
options: transient excludes a specific field from the serialized byte stream entirely (restored to its default value on deserialization), while serialVersionUID is a version identifier checked for class compatibility -- it does not control which fields are written
transient and serialVersionUID both control which fields are skipped during serialization, just at different levels
serialVersionUID marks a field as sensitive so it is encrypted, while transient only affects logging
Declaring serialVersionUID automatically makes every non-primitive field transient by default
explanation: These solve two unrelated problems: transient is a per-field exclusion (used for secrets like passwords or derived values), while serialVersionUID is a single class-level version stamp used to verify that the class reading serialized data is compatible with the class that wrote it -- conflating the two is a common source of confusion.

promptText: Beyond simply being a stereotype for component scanning, what concrete functional behavior does @Repository add that @Component alone does not?
options: @Repository enables exception translation, wrapping low-level, vendor-specific persistence exceptions into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy via a bean post-processor
@Repository forces the annotated bean to be instantiated eagerly at application startup, unlike @Component
@Repository automatically wraps every method call in a database transaction, while @Component and @Service do not
@Repository beans are the only ones visible to Spring's dependency injection container
explanation: All three stereotypes are meta-annotated with @Component and get scanned and registered as beans identically, but @Repository specifically triggers Spring's exception-translation post-processor, converting exceptions like SQLException or Hibernate-specific exceptions into the consistent DataAccessException hierarchy -- a concrete difference many candidates miss when they call the three annotations "basically the same."

promptText: Because of type erasure, why can't you overload a method with parameters `List<String>` and `List<Integer>`, and what does this reveal about generics at runtime?
options: After erasure both parameters become the identical raw type List, so the two "overloads" have the same signature and the compiler rejects it as a duplicate method; at runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` also share the same Class object
The compiler allows the overload but the JVM throws an exception the first time both methods are called in the same program
Generics prevent method overloading entirely, even for parameters of genuinely different raw types
List<String> and List<Integer> retain their distinct type parameters at runtime specifically to support this kind of overload
explanation: Type erasure strips generic type parameters at compile time so that both List<String> and List<Integer> compile down to the same raw List, meaning they share one Class object at runtime and cannot be distinguished via instanceof or reflection -- which is exactly why the compiler treats the two overloads as duplicate signatures rather than distinct methods.

promptText: Given a method `void copyAll(List<? extends Number> src, List<? super Number> dest)`, why does the compiler allow reading elements from `src` as Number but reject calling `src.add(5)`, while it allows `dest.add(5)` but only lets you read elements from `dest` as Object?
options: `? extends Number` only guarantees the list holds SOME subtype of Number the compiler cannot pin down, so adding is unsafe (any concrete subtype could reject the wrong element), while reading as Number is always safe; `? super Number` guarantees a Number can safely be added, but reading only yields the common supertype Object
Both wildcards behave identically; the compiler restriction is arbitrary and exists purely as a style convention (PECS)
`? extends Number` allows both reading and adding freely, while `? super Number` forbids both
The restrictions apply only when the list is a TreeList; ArrayList and LinkedList are exempt from PECS rules
explanation: This is exactly the PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) rule: with `? extends Number` the compiler knows only that the actual list holds some unknown Number subtype, so it cannot guarantee any object you try to add would be compatible, but reading as Number is always safe; with `? super Number` the compiler knows any supertype of Number is present, so adding a Number is always safe, but reading only guarantees an Object came out.

promptText: A JPA entity computes hashCode() from its database-generated `id` field, which is null before the entity is first persisted. Why can adding such an entity to a HashSet before saving it, then saving it, cause it to effectively "disappear" from that HashSet afterward?
options: The entity's hashCode() value changes once the id is assigned by the database, so it now maps to a different bucket than the one it was originally inserted into, and a lookup by the new hashCode will not find the old bucket entry
Hibernate automatically removes any entity from all in-memory HashSets the moment it is persisted
HashSet periodically purges entries whose equals() has not been called recently
The entity's proxy class overrides equals() to always return false once a database transaction commits
explanation: This is a direct, practical consequence of the equals/hashCode contract combined with a mutable hash source: HashSet placed the entity in a bucket based on its hashCode() at insertion time (when id was null); once id is populated and hashCode() is recomputed from it, subsequent contains()/remove() calls compute a different bucket and never find the original entry, effectively orphaning it -- which is why hashCode() should be based on a stable, immutable business key rather than a database-generated id.
